claims.text: The starting CoCrFeNiTi elemental powder mixture is coarse, segregated, and has low lattice strain with no significant grain refinement.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling produces sufficient lattice strain and grain refinement in CoCrFeNiTi.
The milling-induced strain and grain refinement lower the Gibbs free-energy barrier for an FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
SPS at 1000°C densifies the milled CoCrFeNiTi powder.
SPS at 1000°C avoids excessive Ti-driven HCP precipitation in the proposed alloy.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch define a stability window favoring BCC CoCrFeNiTi.
Milling creates a high density of dislocations, stacking faults, and nanocrystalline grains that favors BCC over HCP.
Lattice strain from milling raises internal energy and reduces intrinsic stacking-fault energy.
Stored milling energy combined with the alloy's VEC and atomic-radius mismatch shifts phase stability toward BCC during sintering at 1000°C.
The proposed process will produce porosity below 2%.
The processed alloy will have a single-phase or dominant BCC solid-solution structure.
The processed alloy will have significantly higher Vickers hardness than cast counterparts.
The predicted hardness increase is caused primarily by grain-boundary strengthening.
The processed alloy will avoid detrimental HCP phases and excessive grain growth.
Conventionally cast or briefly milled CoCrFeNiTi typically has low hardness, high porosity, and mixed FCC/BCC/HCP phases.
Above a sintering-temperature threshold, thermal energy causes excessive grain growth that reduces hardness.
Above a sintering-temperature threshold, Ti segregation can thermodynamically re-stabilize an HCP phase.
Prolonged milling can introduce Fe contamination and promote oxide formation.
Low-load Vickers testing at 0.1 kg can isolate grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.
Fe contamination above 2 at.% is an evidence-based upper-bound criterion for failure of the milling window.

contradictions.description: The structural-mediator field says Ti typically stabilizes HCP at lower temperatures, whereas the mechanism and boundary describe HCP precipitation or re-stabilization as occurring after an upper-temperature threshold is exceeded; the uncertainty field separately calls HCP stabilization at 1000°C a risk.
